parts.title: A Home Contents Insurance Quote
parts.scenario: A man who has just moved home phones an insurance company to get a quote for home contents insurance.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Priya
voices.desc: Insurance adviser — female, late 20s, bright, efficient and polite; British accent (southern English)

voices.label: Daniel
voices.desc: Caller — male, late 30s, friendly, slightly hurried, good-humoured; British accent (northern English)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning an insurance company to get a quote for home contents insurance. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 6.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [telephone rings twice, then the line clicks open] [bright, professional] Good afternoon, Hartwell Home Insurance, you're speaking to Priya. How can I help?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [friendly, a little hurried] Oh, hello. I'm after a quote for contents insurance. I've just moved into a new place, and my old policy doesn't transfer, apparently. [light laugh] Which nobody told me.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [warm] That happens a lot, don't worry. I can do a quote for you now, it'll only take ten minutes or so. Could I start with your name?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Yes, it's Daniel Fairleigh.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [typing, careful] Daniel... and the surname, is that F... A... I... R... L... E... Y?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [patient chuckle, used to this] Everyone does that. No, it's F... A... I... R... L... E... I... G... H.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [repeating slowly as she types] L... E... I... G... H. Sorry about that. And the address of the property you'd like insured?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [clearly] Twenty-two Meadowcroft Road, in Selby.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [friendly] And when did you move in?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [laughs] Only last Saturday. There are still boxes absolutely everywhere.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [efficient] Thank you. And what type of property is it? A house, a flat...?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [thinking aloud] Well, the estate agent advertised it as a flat, but it isn't really, because it's on two floors and it's got its own front door. [decisive] It's a maisonette.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [typing] A maisonette, fine. We actually treat those the same as houses. [short pause] And could I ask your occupation? It does make a small difference to the price.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [amused] Does it? Well, I was a teacher for years, chemistry, but I retrained a while back, so I'm a pharmacist now.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [pleasant] Pharmacist, lovely. Now, the total value of your contents. That's basically everything you'd take with you if you moved: furniture, clothes, electrical goods, and so on.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [hesitant] Er, I did try to work it out last night. I came to about thirty thousand pounds.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [gently cautious] Most people underestimate, I'm afraid. Did that include things like clothes, and all your kitchen equipment?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [sighs] Ah... no, it didn't. [short pause] Let's say thirty-eight thousand, to be on the safe side.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [approving] Thirty-eight thousand. That's probably wiser. And is there any single item worth more than two thousand pounds? We'd need to list those separately.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [thinking] Hmm. My bike cost a lot, but it was just under two thousand. I used to have quite a good watch, but I sold that last year. [suddenly remembering] Oh, the telescope! That was about two thousand four hundred.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [typing] A telescope. I'll put that down as a specified item. Last question in this section: have you made any claims on home insurance in the past five years?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [matter-of-fact] Just one. About three years ago a pipe burst in the flat upstairs, and it came through my ceiling.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [checking] Ah. And was that recorded as flood damage, or...?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [firm] No, the insurer was quite clear it wasn't a flood, because that's water coming in from outside. They put it down as water damage.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [efficient] Then that's what I'll put.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [slightly worried] Will a claim like that push the price up much?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [reassuring, honest] A little, but not a great deal, as it wasn't your fault and it was more than two years ago.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 7 to 10.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [brisk, explaining] Right, so based on all that, I can offer you three levels of cover. The first is called Essential.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [wry] The cheapest, I imagine.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [light laugh] That's right. For your property, Essential would be nine pounds eighty-five a month.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [surprised] Oh. I'm sure I saw eight ninety-five on your website.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [apologetic] You may well have, that was the price until the end of last month. It went up on the first, I'm afraid, so it's nine eighty-five now. [clearly] Essential doesn't include accidental damage, and the excess, which is what you'd pay towards any claim yourself, is two hundred and fifty pounds.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [unimpressed] Hmm. That's quite a lot.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [neutral] It is. Then there's Standard, at sixteen pounds forty a month. That does cover accidental damage, so if you spilt paint on the carpet, say, or dropped your laptop. And the excess comes down to a hundred.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [interested] What about things I take out of the house? I carry my laptop to work and back every day.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Standard covers your belongings away from home as well. Some insurers limit that to a thousand pounds, but ours goes up to fifteen hundred pounds.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [thinking aloud] Fifteen hundred. Well, the laptop's worth a lot less than that, so that'd be fine.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [upbeat] And finally there's Premium, which is twenty-three pounds ninety a month. That has everything in Standard, plus a couple of extras.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Such as?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [explaining] Well, people often assume it includes medical cover, but that's really something for travel insurance. What Premium does give you is legal expenses. So if you ended up in a dispute with a builder, for instance, or a neighbour, we'd help with the solicitor's fees.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [dry chuckle] Given my last neighbour, that's quite tempting.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [laughs softly] And the other extra is to do with keys. If your house keys are lost or stolen, we won't just pay for new keys, anyone can get those cut. We pay to have all the locks changed.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [approving] That's sensible, actually. Whoever found them might know the address.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [agreeing] Exactly. Would you like me to email all three quotes so you can compare them properly?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [relieved] Yes, please. I'm leaning towards Standard, to be honest, but I'd like to talk it over with my partner first. [short pause] Is the price fixed if I take a few days?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [reassuring] The quote's valid for thirty days, so there's no rush. And if you pay for the whole year in one go, rather than monthly, it works out about eight per cent cheaper.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: [pleased] Good to know. Thanks very much, Priya, you've been really helpful.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: [warm] My pleasure. The email should be with you in the next few minutes. Goodbye!

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Arriving in Kelmouth
parts.context: Monologue in an everyday social context (1 speaker)
parts.scenario: A coach-tour guide describes the seaside town of Kelmouth to her passengers as the coach arrives.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Guide
voices.desc: Coach-tour guide — female, 50s, cheerful, chatty and experienced, projecting over a microphone; British accent (south-west England)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a tour guide talking to a group of passengers on a coach as they arrive in a seaside town. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 16.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [soft click of a coach microphone] [cheerful, projecting] Right, everyone, welcome to Kelmouth! We've just pulled into the coach park, which, as you can see, is right at the western end of the seafront. Before you all rush off, let me give you a quick idea of where everything is. If you've got the little map I handed out this morning, have it ready.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [clear, orienting] On the map the sea is along the bottom, so north is at the top. The long road running east along the seafront is the Promenade, and about halfway along it you'll see the clock tower. That's the easiest place to get your bearings, because Church Street runs straight up the hill from the clock tower to the Market Square.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [informative] So, first of all, the tourist information centre. Those of you who came on this trip a few years ago might remember it up in the Market Square, next to the church. [short pause] Well, it isn't there any more. That building's the town library now.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [pointing out the route] The centre moved down to the seafront. Walk along the Promenade with the sea on your right. You'll pass the deckchair hire place on the beach side, and the tourist office is just after the clock tower, on your left, looking out over the sand.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [enthusiastic] Now, if you like art, you're in for a treat. Head up Church Street from the clock tower. There's a bank on the corner on your right, [dry aside] which is useful, because a few of the little shops here still won't take cards. But keep going, and about halfway up the hill, on the left, is the Harbour Light Gallery. It's tiny, but it's got some lovely paintings of the coast.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [warm, recommending] At the top of Church Street you come out into the Market Square. The church is straight ahead of you, on the far side, and the building to the right of it is the library I mentioned. For lunch, I'd really recommend The Lobster Pot. People expect it to be on the seafront, but it isn't. It's tucked away in the top left-hand corner of the square, so on the opposite side from the library.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [informative] Back down on the seafront, if you carry on east along the Promenade, you'll come to the harbour. Do visit the lifeboat museum there. [short pause] It used to be out at the very end of the jetty, in the old boathouse, but that was badly damaged in a storm, so now it's on the north side of the harbour, right beside the slipway, where the lifeboats were launched in the old days.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [encouraging] A lot of you were asking about the seal-watching trips. You buy your tickets on board, and the boats don't go from the slipway, because the water there is far too shallow at low tide. They leave from the far end of the jetty instead, so allow a few minutes to walk out there.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [softer, almost confidential] And finally, if you want the best view in Kelmouth, and it's my favourite spot, don't go to the harbour at all. Come back here to the coach park and take the steps at the western end, up onto the headland. At the top of the steps there's a little viewpoint with a bench. On a clear day you can see three lighthouses from there.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 17 to 20.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [practical, friendly] Now, people always ask me about the beach. It did get one of those national awards for clean beaches, but that was a good few years ago, and it lost it last year. Nothing serious, just a paperwork problem, I'm told.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [matter-of-fact] It's usually packed in the mornings, and it doesn't really empty out until about five, so don't expect much peace and quiet after lunch either. [serious, slowing down] What you do need to know is that when the tide's going out, there's a strong current near the rocks. The lifeguards put up red flags then, and nobody should go in the water until they come down.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [storytelling, lively] A little bit of history. Most visitors assume Kelmouth grew rich on fishing. And there were fishing boats, of course, but they only ever really fed the town itself. The money came from slate. It was dug out of the quarries a few miles inland and shipped all over the world from this harbour.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [thoughtful] The railway arrived in the eighteen-seventies and brought the first holidaymakers, but by then the big houses on the hill had already been built. So tourism came later; it wasn't what made the town wealthy.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [enthusiastic, then frank] Now, food. You can't leave Kelmouth without trying a saffron bun. Every café sells them, but, between you and me, the café ones mostly come from a factory up the road. Go to Pengelly's on Church Street instead. They're proper bakers, and they make their own.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [light laugh] People will tell you they have to be eaten warm, but honestly, they're just as good cold. And there's no need to rush over there first thing, either, because they bake all day long.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [firmer, important] Right, now the important bit, so please listen. We'd originally planned to leave at half past five, but the driver has to have the coach back at the depot earlier than we thought, so we'll be leaving at five o'clock sharp instead.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [explaining] We'll go from right here in the coach park, the same spot you're getting off. The driver did think about picking you up by the harbour, but there just isn't room for a coach to turn round there. [wry] And please don't try ringing me if you're running late. The phone signal on this bit of coast is hopeless, so I probably wouldn't get the call anyway.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: [cheerful, wrapping up] So, five o'clock, here. Have a wonderful afternoon, and mind the seagulls if you're eating outside. [laughs] They're bigger than you'd think, and they're not shy!

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

question_groups.instructions: Label the map below. Write the correct letter, A–I, next to Questions 11–16.
question_groups.heading: Kelmouth town centre and seafront
question_groups.layout: Plan of Kelmouth, north at the top. The sea fills the bottom (south) edge, with a strip of beach along it. The Promenade runs west–east along the seafront just above the beach. The Coach Park is at the far west (left) end of the Promenade. A Clock Tower stands on the Promenade about halfway along. Church Street runs north from the Clock Tower up to Market Square at the top centre of the map; St Anne's Church stands on the north (far) side of Market Square, in the middle. The Harbour is at the far east (right) end of the Promenade; a Slipway runs down into the water on the north side of the harbour, and a long Jetty runs south out to sea from the southern side of the harbour. Steps lead up from the western edge of the Coach Park onto a Headland at the far left of the map. Lettered positions: B — on the beach (south) side of the Promenade, between the Coach Park and the Clock Tower. E — on the land (north) side of the Promenade, immediately east of the Clock Tower. F — on the east side of Church Street, on its bottom corner with the Promenade. C — on the west side of Church Street, halfway up. A — in the north-west corner of Market Square, west of the church. G — on the east side of Market Square, immediately to the right of the church. H — on the north side of the Harbour, beside the Slipway. D — at the far (southern) end of the Jetty. I — on the Headland at the top of the Steps, west of the Coach Park.

items.prompt: Art gallery
items.evidence: about halfway up the hill, on the left, is the Harbour Light Gallery
items.trap: F is the bank on the right-hand corner of Church Street.

items.prompt: Recommended restaurant
items.evidence: It's tucked away in the top left-hand corner of the square, so on the opposite side from the library
items.trap: Listeners may expect the seafront, which is rejected, or confuse it with G, the library beside the church.

items.prompt: Lifeboat museum
items.evidence: now it's on the north side of the harbour, right beside the slipway
items.trap: D, the end of the jetty, was its previous location.

items.prompt: Departure point for boat trips
items.evidence: They leave from the far end of the jetty instead
items.trap: The slipway (H) is mentioned and rejected as too shallow.

items.prompt: Viewpoint
items.evidence: take the steps at the western end, up onto the headland. At the top of the steps there's a little viewpoint
items.trap: The harbour is mentioned and rejected ('don't go to the harbour at all').

question_groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.prompt: What does the guide say about Kelmouth's beach?

options.A: Bathing is dangerous at certain stages of the tide.
options.B: It has been recognised for its cleanliness this year.
options.C: It becomes much quieter after midday.

items.evidence: when the tide's going out, there's a strong current near the rocks
items.trap: B: the award was won years ago and lost last year; C: it doesn't empty out until about five.

items.prompt: According to the guide, the town's wealth originally came from

options.B: the export of a building material.

items.evidence: The money came from slate. It was dug out of the quarries a few miles inland and shipped all over the world
items.trap: Fishing 'only ever really fed the town' and tourism came after the town was already wealthy.

items.prompt: What advice does the guide give about saffron buns?

options.A: Buy them from a shop that produces them on the premises.
options.B: Eat them while they are still hot.
options.C: Go early in the day before they sell out.

items.evidence: They're proper bakers, and they make their own
items.trap: B: she says they're just as good cold; C: there's no need to rush because they bake all day.

items.prompt: What are passengers told about the return journey?

options.A: The pick-up point has been moved.
options.B: The departure time is earlier than planned.
options.C: Passengers who are delayed should phone her.

items.evidence: we'll be leaving at five o'clock sharp instead
items.trap: A: the harbour pick-up was considered but rejected; C: she asks them not to ring her.

parts.title: Case Study: A Failed Product Launch
parts.scenario: Two business students, Leah and Owen, discuss with their tutor a case study about a cycle manufacturer's unsuccessful launch of an electric bike.
parts.accent: Tutor British (en-GB); Leah Canadian (en-CA); Owen British (en-GB)

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Dr Morgan
voices.desc: Business tutor — female, 50s, warm but probing, precise; British accent (RP)

voices.label: Leah
voices.desc: Student — female, early 20s, thoughtful, articulate, quietly confident; Canadian accent

voices.label: Owen
voices.desc: Student — male, early 20s, enthusiastic, quick to jump in, good at conceding; British accent (Midlands)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two business students, Leah and Owen, talking to their tutor about a case study of a product launch that failed. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 24.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [a door closes softly] [warm, brisk] Come in, both of you, have a seat. So, you've been working on the Calder Cycles case. How are you getting on with it? The presentation's in three weeks, so let's use today to check your main arguments.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [enthusiastic] Really well, actually. It's much more interesting than the one we did last term.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [pleased] Good. Leah, what struck you first when you read it?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [thoughtful] Well, I expected the launch budget to be enormous, and it was, but for a national campaign that's pretty normal. And I knew Calder had done really well with their road bikes, which is presumably why they were so confident. [emphatic] What I genuinely didn't see coming was that the Glide was off the market after only eight months.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [agreeing] Mm. Most firms would give a new product at least two or three years to find its feet.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [jumping in] And that's partly what made us look at their market research.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: Go on.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [confident] Well, some people in our seminar said it was out of date, but it wasn't, they did it the year before launch, which seems fine. And yes, it cost a fortune, but that's not really the point. [slightly incredulous] The problem was who they asked. They surveyed their existing customers, who are mostly serious club cyclists, and they're exactly the people who'd never dream of buying an electric bike.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [dry] Right. They basically asked the wrong crowd.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [measured] I'd agree with that. What about the price? That's what students usually blame first.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [hesitant] We did wonder about that. Should they have launched it cheaper?

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [considered] Well, let's be accurate. It wasn't priced in line with its rivals; it was about four hundred pounds more than the nearest competitor. So I wouldn't call it a bargain. But would a lower launch price have saved it? I doubt it. In the one month they discounted it heavily, sales hardly moved. [firm] So, in my view, it isn't the price that sank it.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [conceding] Fair enough.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: And the timing of the launch?

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [slightly sheepish] I was going to say autumn was the wrong season to launch a bike. Nobody buys one in October.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [gently disagreeing] But the case gives figures for that, Owen. E-bike sales don't really drop in the autumn, because people buy them for commuting, not for fun.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [reluctant] Hmm, okay, true. And the launch had already been put back from June, but a few months' delay isn't unusual, is it?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [decisive] No. What really hurt them was that Voltra brought out its cheaper model just three weeks before.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [agreeing] Yeah, that's what did the damage. I think we're both agreed on that.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [approving] I'd go along with that. And Calder knew Voltra's model was coming, too; it had been in the trade press for months. They just assumed their brand name would carry them.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 25 to 30.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [moving things along] Right, now your problem analysis. The case lists six main problems. Let's go through what you think caused each one. Start with the late deliveries to the shops.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [thinking aloud] Well, my first thought was that the production schedule was just unrealistic.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [doubtful] Was it, though? Have a look at the factory figures in the appendix.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [realising] Oh. They actually hit every production target, so the bikes were ready on time. It's just that nobody told the warehouse the launch date had changed, so no transport had been booked. [short pause] So really, sales and logistics simply weren't talking to each other.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [nodding along] Fair enough.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: Next, the complaints about the battery.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [confident] Now this one I'm sure was the supplier. They switched to a different battery maker about six months before launch.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [politely disagreeing] I thought that too at first, but the case says the new batteries actually did better in lab tests than the old ones. The issue was that every trial ride took place in summer. Nobody had ridden one in cold, wet weather, and that's when the range just collapsed.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [wry] Which, in Britain, is rather a large oversight.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [conceding] Yeah, okay. So they hadn't tried it out properly on actual roads in all seasons.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: And the online reviews?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [dry, wincing] Those were brutal.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [explaining] You'd expect them to be about the battery again, but most of them weren't, actually. The ads said you could go a hundred kilometres on one charge, and the reviewers were getting about sixty.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: So people felt the marketing had promised far more than the bike could deliver.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [wry] And reviewers don't forgive that. Once a few of those went up, the star rating never recovered.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [probing] What about the poor sales through independent bike shops?

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [tentative] Was it because Calder was pushing people to buy direct from their website, so the shops resented it?

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [firm] No, they only started selling online after the shops had given up on it. When customers were interviewed, the main complaint was that shop assistants couldn't answer basic questions, about charging, the motor, anything. Calder never ran a single session to show them the product.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [approving] Quite right. And independent shops were supposed to bring in forty per cent of sales, so that really mattered. [short pause] Then there's the high rate of returns.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: That was mostly faulty brakes, wasn't it?

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [explaining] Right, and that goes back to the factory after all. The board insisted on launching in time for the big trade show, so the assembly line had half the usual time to build the first batch. Things got rushed, and the brakes weren't fitted properly.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [thoughtful] So the factory did meet the target, but at a price.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [emphatic] Exactly. The date they'd been given was never achievable in the first place.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: And finally, the launch going over budget.

script.speaker: Owen
script.text: [hesitant] I assumed the new battery supplier had charged more.

script.speaker: Leah
script.text: [correcting him] They were cheaper, actually, that was half the reason Calder switched. The overspend was mostly because the motors came from Japan and were priced in yen, and the pound fell sharply that spring, so every motor cost them about fifteen per cent more than they'd budgeted for.

script.speaker: Dr Morgan
script.text: [pleased] Exactly. Something completely outside their control, which is worth stressing in your presentation. [brisk] Right, good work, both of you. Let's meet again next Thursday.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: The Printing Press and the Spread of Literacy
parts.scenario: A history lecturer gives a talk on the invention of the printing press and how reading spread in early modern Europe.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Lecturer
voices.desc: History lecturer — male, 50s, engaging, articulate, slightly wry; British accent (RP)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the printing press and the spread of literacy in early modern Europe. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture hall, a faint murmur fading] [engaging, clear] Good morning. Today we're looking at one of the most celebrated inventions in European history, the printing press, and at a question that's much harder to answer than it looks: did printing actually make people literate?

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] Let's start with what came before. There's a popular image of books being copied by monks in candlelit monasteries. And that image used to be accurate, say, in the eleventh century. [short pause] But by the fifteenth century, most copying had moved out of the monasteries altogether. It was done in commercial workshops, and these were clustered around the universities, because that's where the demand for texts was.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [brisk] So there was already a book trade. What Johannes Gutenberg did, in Mainz, around fourteen-fifty, was make it dramatically faster. But it's worth being precise about what he invented, because it wasn't the press. Presses had been used for centuries to squeeze grapes for wine and olives for oil, and he simply adapted one.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining carefully] Nor was movable type entirely new: it had been used in Korea and China long before. His real breakthrough was the hand mould. This was a small, adjustable device that allowed a worker to cast thousands of identical metal letters very quickly, all exactly the same height, so they could be locked together into a page.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [emphatic, slowing down] The effect on speed was staggering. A skilled scribe might need several months to copy a single book. In the same time, a small print shop with three or four workers could produce several hundred copies, and every one of them would be identical, errors included.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful] He also had to solve a problem with ink. The water-based inks that scribes had always used simply ran off metal type. So he turned instead to an oil-based ink, much closer to the varnishes that painters were using at the time. [light, aside] The Flemish painters had been experimenting with oils for a generation, so the knowledge was there.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [wry] Now, you might assume the Bible was the bread and butter of the early printers. It wasn't. The famous Gutenberg Bible was a prestige project, and it very nearly bankrupted him. [emphatic] The steady money came from indulgences. These were single printed sheets, certificates sold by the Church that promised forgiveness of sins, and printers turned them out by the tens of thousands.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Printing spread remarkably fast. By fifteen hundred there were presses in more than two hundred and fifty towns. But it didn't spread evenly. Printers needed customers, so they followed the money, along the main trade routes, and above all to cities that held the great annual fairs, like Frankfurt and Lyon, where they could sell their stock to dealers from all over Europe.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [slightly amused] Interestingly, university towns weren't nearly as attractive to printers as you'd expect. Their demand was steady, but it was small.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] Venice is the classic example. It had no great university to speak of, but it was the commercial capital of the Mediterranean, and by fifteen hundred it had more printers than any other city in Europe.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [building, more animated] The real test of printing's power came in fifteen-seventeen, with Martin Luther. His arguments against the Church spread faster than anything had spread before, and one reason is the language he chose. Scholarly debate was conducted in Latin, but Luther wrote his pamphlets in the vernacular. [clarifying] That's the ordinary language people actually spoke at home, in his case German.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] And these pamphlets were short, cheap and often illustrated, so even people who couldn't read could have them read aloud to them. Which brings us to literacy itself.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [posing a problem] How do historians actually measure literacy in a period with no censuses and no exams? School records barely survive, so they can't be used. Instead, historians count signatures, mostly in marriage registers, where the bride and groom either wrote their names or simply made a mark.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [cautionary] But there's a serious flaw in this method. In this period, reading was taught first, and writing only later, if at all. Plenty of people could read perfectly well but never learned to write. So signature counts almost certainly underestimate how many people could read.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] Even so, the trend is clear. In England, perhaps one man in ten could sign his name around fifteen hundred. By seventeen hundred it was closer to one in two, though the figure was much higher in towns than in the countryside.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [emphatic] This is especially true for women. Girls were rarely kept at school for long. Most learned to read at home, and generally not from a priest or a private tutor, as is sometimes claimed, but from their mothers. So female reading ability is almost invisible in the records.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [conversational] So what did ordinary people read? Not the classics, I'm afraid. In many households the most widely owned printed book wasn't even the Bible. It was the almanac, a cheap booklet bought every year, with a calendar, the dates of markets, weather predictions and advice on farming.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [light laugh] Its predictions were often wildly wrong, of course, but people kept buying it, and for many families it was the first thing they ever learned to read.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful] Ballads and chapbooks, which were little paper-covered storybooks, were enormously popular too, but they tended to be passed around and read until they fell apart, rather than kept on a shelf.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [concluding, reflective] Finally, the long-term effect on language itself. Printing is often credited with fixing English grammar. In fact, grammar changed rather little because of it. What printers did gradually standardise was spelling. A printer selling books across a whole country needed consistent forms, and over a couple of centuries, the endless local variations slowly disappeared.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [wrapping up] So, did printing make people literate? Not on its own. It made reading matter cheap and plentiful, but schooling, religion and trade did much of the rest. We'll pick that up next week.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.
